blocks.text: as the poet has it, and so utterly foreign to those most tender affections with which a mother burns for her offspring. Hence Antoninus Liberalis, Fable [III, 67] 21, rightly writes that the vulture is πάντων ὀρνίθων ἔχθιστον θεοῖς τε, καὶ ἀνθρώποις· καὶ διὰ παντὸς ἵμερον αὐτῷ κρέως καὶ αἵματος ἐνέβαλον ἀνθρωπείου [pantōn ornithōn echthiston theois te, kai anthrōpois; kai dia pantos himeron autō kreōs kai haimatos enebalon anthrōpeiou], of all birds the most hateful to gods and men; in which (the gods) implanted a perpetual craving for human flesh and blood. Indeed, in Photius, Author 223, Theodore, or rather Diodorus, bishop of Tarsus, denies that the vulture feeds its young. Διὰ τί δέ τινα τῶν ζώων [Dia ti de tina tōn zōōn], he says, οὐ τρέφει τὰ γεννήματα, ὥσπερ πτηνῶν γύπας, καὶ κόρακες; [ou trephei ta gennēmata, hōsper ptēnōn gypas, kai korakes?] Why do some animals not feed their offspring, as among birds vultures and ravens? And below: Τίς δὲ κόρακας, καὶ γύπας ἐδίδαξεν ἵπτασθαι· οὓς οὐδὲ τρέφειν οἱ γεγεννηκότες πεφύκασι; [Tis de korakas, kai gypas edidaxen hiptasthai; hous oude trephein hoi gegennēkotes pephykasi?] Who taught ravens or vultures to fly, whom their parents are not even accustomed to feed? But these objections will be refuted with no trouble.

Among the Arabs, they say, رخم [rakham] racham is نسر [nasr] neser, that is, the eagle, not the vulture. We answer that some Arabs, though not all, define it so. For Damir expressly says الرخمه طاير ابقع يشبه النسر في الخلقة [al-rakhma ṭāyir abqaʿ yushbih al-nasr fī al-khilqa]: The rachama is a variegated bird, approaching the nature of the eagle. Thus in Damir's opinion it is not the same bird as the eagle, but merely similar to it. This is most true of the vulture, of which Philes says:
Οὗ τήν τε κεφαλήν γε, βασιλεῦ, καὶ τὸ στόμα, Κἂν μακρόθεν βλέπῃ τις, αἰετὸν λέγει· [Hou tēn te kephalēn ge, basileu, kai to stoma, Kan makrothen blepē tis, aieton legei;]

Whose head and beak, O king, if anyone sees them from afar, he calls it an eagle. Especially among the kinds of eagle, the percnopteri have a vulture-like appearance. Hence they are called γυπαίετοι [gypaietoi], vulture-eagles. Aristotle, History, book 9, chapter 32: Ἔστι δ᾽ ἕτερον γένος (ἀετῶν) περκνόπτερος, etc. γυπὶ ὅμοιος· ὀρειπέλαργος καλεῖται, καὶ γυπαίετος [Esti d᾽ heteron genos (aetōn) perknopteros, etc. gypi homoios; oreipelargos kaleitai, kai gypaietos]. Pliny, book 10, chapter 3: Of the fourth (eagle) kind is the percnopterus, also called oripelargus, of vulture-like appearance. Others call them aegypii. Aelian, History, book 2, chapter 46: Τοὺς δὲ αἰγυπιοὺς, ἐν μεθορίῳ γυπῶν ὄντας καὶ αἰετῶν [Tous de aigypious, en methoriō gypōn ontas kai aietōn]: The aegypii, which are intermediate between vultures and eagles. Moreover, great writers hold that eagles, through mixed mating, at length degenerate into vultures. Pliny: Sea eagles have no kind of their own, but are born from the mixed mating of eagles. What is born of them in turn has its kind among the ossifrages, from which smaller vultures are produced; and from these the great ones, which do not breed at all. This is taken from these words of Aristotle's Marvels: Ἐκ τοῦ [col. 314] ζεύγους δὲ τῶν ἀετῶν θάτερον τῶν ἀγόνων ἁλιαίετος γίνεται παραλλὰξ, ἕως ἂν σύζυγα γένηται, ἐκ δὲ τούτων οἱ περκνοὶ, καὶ γῦπες. οὗτοι δὲ οὐκέτι διορίζουσι περὶ τοὺς γύπας, ἀλλὰ γεννῶσι τοὺς μεγάλους γύπας· οὗτοι δ᾽ εἰσὶν ἄγονοι· [Ek tou zeugous de tōn aetōn thateron tōn agonōn haliaietos ginetai parallax, heōs an syzyga genētai, ek de toutōn hoi perknoi, kai gypes. houtoi de ouketi diorizousi peri tous gypas, alla gennōsi tous megalous gypas; houtoi d᾽ eisin agonoi;] But Pliny rendered this passage of Aristotle in such a way that whatever was difficult (namely the words θάτερον τῶν ἀγόνων [thateron tōn agonōn] and παραλλὰξ ἕως ἂν σύζυγα γένηται [parallax heōs an syzyga genētai]) he skipped over with a carefree leap. [III, 68] I think the first words, namely θάτερον τῶν ἀγόνων [thateron tōn agonōn], are corrupt, and that θάτερον τῶν ἀγενῶν [thateron tōn agenōn] should be read instead, so that the sense of the whole passage is: "From a pair of eagles, one ignoble chick is born in alternation, namely the sea eagle. And when σύζυγα [syzyga] have been born, that is, two degenerate eagles, or two sea eagles, from them are born ossifrages; from the ossifrages, percni and vultures, whose kind changes no further. For these beget other vultures, but larger and sterile ones." Since it follows from what has been said that there is a close kinship between eagles and vultures, no one will be surprised that these birds are often confused by writers and one taken for the other. To prove this by examples: that the liver of Prometheus was devoured by an eagle is related by Hesiod, Theogony, verse 523; Aeschylus in Prometheus Bound, verse 996; Apollonius, Argonautica, book 2, verse 1254, and book 3, verse 851; Accius in Prometheus; Apollodorus, books 1 and 2; Diodorus, book 4; Philostratus, book 2; Plutarch in the book On Rivers, under Phasis; Lucian in Prometheus and in Sacrifices; Pherecydes, book 2; Agroetas in Scythica, book 13; Duris and Herodorus in the Scholiast on Apollonius; Servius on Virgil's sixth Eclogue, etc. Yet Fulgentius, in book 2 of the Mythologies, describes to us Prometheus offering his ever-renewed liver to a fierce vulture, and cites as authorities Nicagoras in the book Distemithea (I read On Prometheus), Aristoxenus in the book of Epimetheia, and Petronius Arbiter in these Hendecasyllables:

The vulture that roams through the depths of the liver ^{a)}, and tears at the breast and the innermost fibres, is not the one the idle ^{b)} poets speak of, but the evils of the heart: envy and excess.
